bio.en: Peter Deng is one of the most under-the-radar impactful product leaders in tech, having been VP of Product at OpenAI - where he oversaw ChatGPT Enterprise, voice, memory, and custom GPTs - and the first Head of Product at Instagram, plus leadership roles at Meta, Uber, and AOL.
bio.zh: Peter Deng 是科技圈最低调却最具影响力的产品领袖之一：曾任 OpenAI 产品副总裁（统管 ChatGPT Enterprise、语音、记忆与自定义 GPT），也是 Instagram 首任产品负责人，并曾在 Meta、Uber 和 AOL 担任领导职务。

summary.en: Peter reflects on what it takes to build products from idea to billions of users, arguing that sometimes the product doesn't matter as much as price and ETA did at Uber. He shares his view that the best product people operate autonomously - if he's still telling you what to do in six months, he hired the wrong person - and discusses the five types of product managers. The conversation also covers the rising importance of AI integrations and what founders should know about building agentic products.
summary.zh: Peter 反思了如何将一个产品从想法做到数十亿用户，提出在 Uber 时真正决定成败的往往是价格与到达时间，而非产品本身。他分享了自己的理念：最优秀的产品人才能够自主运作——如果六个月后他还在告诉你该做什么，那就说明招错了人——并讨论了产品经理的五种类型。对话还涉及日益重要的 AI 集成，以及创始人构建智能体（agentic）产品时必须了解的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You built and led Facebook news feeds. You shipped the Messenger app as its own app. You launched ChatGPT Enterprise. What's an important lesson you've learned about what it takes to succeed building something from idea to one to billions?
turns.zh: 你打造并领导了 Facebook 的新闻流。你把 Messenger 应用独立拆分出来发布。你推出了 ChatGPT Enterprise。关于从想法到一、再到数十亿规模做成一件事，你学到的最重要的一课是什么？

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: You have to plan your chess moves out in advance. You have to really think before you act and build systems that were going to let you go sustainably faster.
turns.zh: 你必须提前规划好你的"棋步"。你必须真正谋定而后动，并建立一套能让你持续加速的系统。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's the most counterintuitive lesson you've learned?
turns.zh: 你学到的最反直觉的一课是什么？

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: Sometimes your product actually doesn't matter. At Uber, I learned this because, really, the price and the ETA at Uber was the product. Looking at it from a holistic perspective, we humans consume the entirety of the product. It's not to say that you shouldn't fix the bug, but it doesn't have as much of an impact as something that is more important to people.
turns.zh: 有时候你的产品其实根本不重要。在 Uber，我学到了这一点，因为说真的，Uber 的"价格"和"预计到达时间（ETA）"才是产品。从整体的角度来看，我们人类消费的是产品的全部。这并不是说你不该修那个 bug，而是它带来的影响和那些对用户更重要的事情相比，没那么大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's one specific thing you think will change in a big way with AI that people don't think enough about?
turns.zh: 你认为 AI 会带来什么具体而重大、但人们思考得还不够多的改变？

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: Education is going to change. My son, he was nine at the time, built a custom GPT that you can type in any topic and it would give you a sentence that had every letter of the English alphabet. Isn't that mind-blowing? I can already see his brain rewiring.
turns.zh: 教育将会改变。我儿子当时九岁，他做了一个自定义的 GPT：你输入任意主题，它就能生成一句包含英文字母表里每一个字母的话。这难道不让人震惊吗？我已经能看到他的大脑在重新连接。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's one thing you look for in people you hire?
turns.zh: 你在招人时看重对方身上的哪一点？

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: In 6 months, if I'm telling you what to do, I've hired the wrong person. It helps me and the person operate on a different level where the goal is not, did you hit this OKR? The Meta goal becomes, are we calibrating enough? Are we actually getting into a spot where in 6 months you're the one telling me what needs to be done?
turns.zh: 如果六个月后还是我在告诉你该做什么，那我就招错人了。这能让我和对方在一个不同的层面上协作——我们的目标不是"你有没有完成这个 OKR？"，更高的目标变成：我们校准得够不够？我们是不是已经到了这样一种状态——六个月后，是由你来告诉我该做什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's something you've learned about what it takes to be a great product person?
turns.zh: 要做好一个产品人，你学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: I think there are five different types of product managers. Number one is-
turns.zh: 我觉得产品经理有五种不同的类型。第一种是——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Today my guest is Peter Deng. Peter is maybe the most under the radar impactful Product Leader that you have never heard of. I often say that the best product people are not the people on Twitter and LinkedIn sharing advice, but the people who don't have time to do that because they're too busy doing the work. Peter is the epitome of this. He was VP of product at OpenAI where he oversaw product design and engineering for ChatGPT and helped ship ChatGPT Enterprise, voice, memory, desktop, custom GPTs and more. He also oversaw and built their first growth team. He was the first Head of Product at Instagram where he worked closely with Mike and Kevin, and oversaw all product development, including on content sharing, ads, growth, even helped build out their design and user research functions. He was also a Head of the Rider product team at Uber where he oversaw everything in the Rider app, including big improvements to pickups and drop-offs at Uber Pool and airports. (00:02:18): He also helped the team launch new products including Uber Reserve, which is now approaching a $5 billion a year business. He also spent nearly 10 years at Facebook as their 4th ever Product Manager where he built and led the team behind the current Newsfeed product, the standalone Messenger app, also photos, and groups, and homepage, and profiles. He was also Chief Product Officer at Airtable where he helped the company systemize how they built products and transitioned to Enterprise. He also led product management at Oculus. These days he is General Partner at Felicis where he is able to bring everything he's learned to more founders as an investor. He has never done a podcast before or shared any of these lessons or stories publicly. So, you are in for a real treat. Check it out at lennysnewsletter.com and click bundle. With that, I bring you Peter Deng. turns.en: Hey Lenny. Thanks for having me.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, integrations have become a big deal for AI products. Why is that?
turns.zh: 那么，集成（integrations）对 AI 产品来说已经变得非常重要。为什么会这样？

turns.speaker: Brandon Foo
turns.en: Integrations are mission-critical for AI for two reasons: First, AI products need contacts from their customer's business data such as Google Drive files, Slack messages or CRM records. Second, for AI products to automate work on behalf of users, AI agents need to be able to take action across these different third-party tools.
turns.zh: 集成对 AI 至关重要，原因有二：第一，AI 产品需要来自客户业务数据的内容，比如 Google Drive 文件、Slack 消息或 CRM 记录。第二，要让 AI 产品替用户自动化工作，AI 智能体必须能够跨各种第三方工具采取行动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, where does Paragon fit into all this?

turns.speaker: Brandon Foo
turns.en: Well, these integrations are a pain to build, and that's why Paragon provides an embedded platform that enables engineers to ship these product integrations in just days instead of months across every use case from RAG data ingestion to a Agentic actions.
turns.zh: 嗯，这些集成做起来很痛苦，所以 Paragon 提供了一个嵌入式平台，让工程师只需几天而不是几个月，就能交付这些产品集成，覆盖从 RAG 数据摄取到智能体（Agentic）操作的各种场景。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I know from firsthand experience that maintenance is even harder than just building it for the first time.
turns.zh: 而我根据 firsthand 经验知道，维护比第一次搭建还要难。

turns.speaker: Brandon Foo
turns.en: Exactly. And we believe product teams should focus engineering efforts and competitive advantages, not integrations. That's why companies like U.COM, AI21 and hundreds of others use Paragon to accelerate their integration strategy.
turns.zh: 没错。我们相信产品团队应该把工程精力放在竞争优势上，而不是集成上。这正是 U.COM、AI21 等数百家公司使用 Paragon 来加速其集成策略的原因。

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: Thank you. I'm so thrilled to be here, really honored. Looking forward to having a great time here.
turns.zh: 谢谢。我真的很激动能来，深感荣幸。期待今天聊得尽兴。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As we were preparing for this conversation, we were jamming on what we should focus on. There's so much that we're going to talk about. But something that you said was really interesting and I'm really excited to start with this, which is that, you've always felt that you haven't been able to say all the things you really think and feel because you've been within corporations, PR people keeping you on message, and this is the first time that you feel free to share.
turns.zh: 在我们准备这次对话时，我们一直在碰撞该聚焦什么。要聊的太多了。但你说的一件事特别有意思，我也很兴奋想从这个开始——那就是，你一直觉得自己因为身处大公司、有 PR 人员让你保持"口径一致"，而从未能说出自己真正所思所感，而这是你第一次感到可以自由分享了。

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: First time.
turns.zh: 第一次。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so first of all, just how does that feel? Second of all, tell us something that you've been wanting to share or that you can finally talk about.
turns.zh: 好，那么首先，这到底是什么感觉？其次，告诉我们一些你一直想分享、现在终于能开口说的事。

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: Well, it feels really good. So, let me ask... I love it that you're starting with a spicy question here and let me share some more context behind it. I'm here to speak more freely, but it's not really what you think. I'm not here to divulge any secrets from the companies. But naturally I'm kind of a storyteller, I'm kind of an introvert. So, this podcast, I feel like I have the ability to go deeper with you on any topic and kind of add the context. Because I think without some of the context, some of my spicy takes or whatnot might be taken out of context, and just not having the time pressure, not feeling like there's some PR message I have to hit, is just really freeing. So, it feels awesome, really anything that is on your mind that you should find interesting to your listeners, I'm here for it and yeah, I'm excited.
turns.zh: 嗯，感觉真的很好。让我先说……我很喜欢你一上来就抛个"带劲"的问题，让我再多交代点背景。我来这里是想更自由地表达，但不是你想的那样。我不是来泄露各家公司的秘密的。只是我骨子里算个讲故事的人，也算个内向的人。所以在这档播客里，我觉得自己能和你就任何话题聊得更深，并补充背景。因为我觉得如果没有一些背景，我那些"带劲"的观点可能会被断章取义；而没有任何时间压力、也不觉得非得去击中某个 PR 口径，这真的让人如释重负。所以感觉太棒了——任何你心里觉得听众会感兴趣的东西，我都在这儿奉陪，是的，我很兴奋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something I always tell guests, and I don't want people to take this out of context also, but I always describe myself as a reverse journalist where I want the guests to be the best version of themselves. I never want to catch people off guard or just say something they never meant to say. So-
turns.zh: 有件事我常对嘉宾说，而且我也不希望别人曲解我的意思——我总把自己描述成"反向记者"，我想让嘉宾展现出最好的自己。我绝不想让人措手不及，或说出他们从没想过要说的话。所以——

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: That's great.
turns.zh: 那很好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... it's a safe space. Okay. But still, is there anything that you want to share or that might be interesting to share that you've been wanting to share that you haven't been able to? Is there anything along those lines?
turns.zh: ……这是个安全的空间。好。但话说回来，有没有什么是你想分享、或觉得值得分享、却一直没机会说的？有这方面的东西吗？

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: I mean, I always get this question around sort of, AGI, is it coming? Is it going to solve everything?
turns.zh: 嗯，我老被问到这类问题，大概是关于 AGI——它会不会来？它是不是能解决一切？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What have you seen?
turns.zh: 你亲眼看到了什么？

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: I mean, it's so interesting because when I was at OpenAI, it was around the time that people were really scared of AI and, "Oh, it's going to get rid of humans or it's going to do all these things." But with every technology, I think everyone's been just kind of taking some time to acclimate to it. And I think with AGI it's a similar thing, which is it's so far out that everyone's like, "Well, what's our world going to be like?" And the real answer is none of us really know. But in terms of solving problems, I think some people believe AGI is going to solve everything, but I don't think so. AGI is just necessary but not sufficient. A lot of the value is still going to require a bunch of hustle from a lot of builders to really turn that new source of energy and channel it into something that we humans want to use that solves some of our problems. And that hustle is going to be required, that elbow grease is going to be required to really make AGI something useful.
turns.zh: 嗯，这很有意思，因为我在 OpenAI 时，正是人们真的害怕 AI 的时候，"哦，它会取代人类，会做所有这些事"。但每一项技术出现，大家都需要一点时间去适应。我觉得 AGI 也是一样——它太遥远，以至于大家都在想"那我们的世界会变成什么样？"而真正的答案是，没人真正知道。但就解决问题而言，有人觉得 AGI 会解决一切，我并不这么认为。AGI 只是必要条件，而非充分条件。大量的价值仍然需要大量建设者付出一番拼搏，才能真正把这种新能量引导成我们想要使用、能解决部分问题的东西。那种拼搏、那种苦功夫，是让 AGI 变得有用所必需的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Your point is that people think AGI hits, all of a sudden all jobs are gone, AGI is doing everything. Because I think this is a optimistic message that things will be okay if AGI, basically AGI being, and I'm curious if you have a clear definition, but AGI being, AI being just basically as smart as humans-
turns.zh: 你的意思是，人们以为 AGI 一到来，工作就全没了，AGI 包揽一切。因为我觉得这是一个乐观的信息：即便 AGI——基本上 AGI 指的是 AI 聪明得和人类不相上下——我也好奇你有没有清晰的定义——

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: Look, I won't-
turns.zh: 听着，我不会——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... generally.
turns.zh: ……大致上。

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: ... claim to be an expert on this at all, but I think that with every technology that's come out, we've been able to harness it and it takes a lot of harnessing. I think I'm going to use that word very deliberately. I'll use something really basic. What seems obvious today is that, there was a time when databases were all the rage. It's like, "Oh my goodness, you can store a bunch of data and you can query it really quickly and imagine all the possibilities." And I think that a lot of amazing entrepreneurs and builders built some really great products on top of databases.
turns.zh: ……自诩为这方面的专家。但我觉得，每一项问世的技术，我们都能驾驭它，而这需要大量的"驾驭"。我故意要用这个词。我打个很基础的比方。今天看来显而易见的是，曾几何时数据库风靡一时。"天哪，你能存一堆数据，还能飞快地查询，想想有多少可能性。"而很多了不起的创业者和建设者，正是基于数据库打造了很棒的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: In fact, that's kind of the basis of all the stuff that we're seeing today. And it seems so obvious today, but I don't know, maybe in 10 years, 15 years when we look back, it's like, "Of course it made sense that we have this super intelligent thinking machine." But it requires the product builders to be able to go in there and say, "How do we channel this energy to make it something that we as humans love to use and want to use?"
turns.zh: 事实上，那正是我们今天看到的一切的基础。今天它显得如此理所当然，但我不知道，也许 10 年、15 年后回看，会是"我们拥有这台超级智能的思考机器，当然合情合理"。但它需要产品建设者能够深入其中，去思考"我们如何引导这股能量，让它变成我们人类喜欢用、愿意用的东西？"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love the optimism around this. It's just like things will not go crazy once computers are as generally intelligent as humans.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这种乐观。就像是说，一旦计算机达到人类水平的通用智能，事情也不会失控。

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: I think that's exactly what I'm trying to say. And I think that again, every technology people have this fear. And I remember watching a documentary once and they were talking about how when the bicycle came out, people were like, "Oh my goodness, this is going to be the end of all things." And again, it sounds silly today. Because you're like, "bicycles, really?" But then if you put yourself in the context and the mindset of a previous generation, which the next generation will be looking back at this podcast in that previous generation, I think that again, I think optimistically, things are going to be okay, we're going to adapt. And this was actually one of the things that I talked about with my friend Josh Constine at South by Southwest, is this idea that humans will always co-evolve with technology. And I think that that co-evolution is already happening. (00:10:55): If you take a look at, there was a lot of a fear of AI just when ChatGPT came out, but when you start to get familiar with it things, that kind of things change and then you are able to evolve from being fearful to familiar and to go all the way to having this mastery of this thing of like, "Oh my goodness, look at all the startups that are happening now. All the things that we can build. And just over 18 months." I would say we look back and there's been an attitude shift. And so I guess part of my optimism comes from, if you look back 18 months and you look forward 18 months, might it be the same thing for something that we're chasing now?
turns.zh: 我想说的正是这个。而且我觉得，每一项技术人们都会有这种恐惧。我记得看过一部纪录片，讲自行车刚问世时，人们说"天哪，这会毁掉一切"。今天听来很可笑，因为你会想"自行车？真的吗？"但如果你把自己代入上一代人的语境和心态——下一代人会像看上一代人一样回看这档播客——我觉得，乐观地看，事情会好起来的，我们会适应。这其实也是我和朋友 Josh Constine 在西南偏南（South by Southwest）聊过的一点：人类总会与技术共同进化。而我认为这种共同进化已经在发生了。(00:10:55): 你看，ChatGPT 刚出来时大家很恐惧 AI，但当你开始熟悉它，事情就变了，你就能从恐惧演进到熟悉，再一路走到真正驾驭它——"天哪，看看现在涌出的这么多创业公司。我们能构建的一切。仅仅 18 个月。"可以说回看这 18 个月，态度已经转变了。所以我乐观的一部分来源是：如果你回看 18 个月、再往前看 18 个月，我们现在追逐的东西，会不会也是同样的情形？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, let me follow this AI thread a little bit more and then we can move on to other things. I feel like every conversation, there's a time to AI conversation and then it's like, okay, there's other things that also matter. So, let me ask you this, the question, what's one specific thing you think will change in a big way with AI that people don't think enough about?
turns.zh: 好，让我再顺着 AI 这条线多聊一点，然后我们转到别的话题。我觉得每段对话都有个聊 AI 的时候，然后就像"好，其他重要的事也该谈谈了"。那么我问你这个问题：你认为 AI 会带来什么具体而重大、但人们思考得还不够多的改变？

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: I think education is going to change in a big way. And I think a lot about this because I'm involved in my kid's school quite a bit, and that's something I've done after I left OpenAI. And what's fascinating to me is that watching my son who got to dog food, a bunch of the OpenAI stuff before it was public, I think I can safely say that, that seems okay. And when he was playing with ChatGPT and some of the latest models and he was nine at the time, I can already see his brain rewiring. He was starting to ask questions and he never heard the word prompt before, but he's like, just this is how awesome the human mind is, because he was exposed to this technology at an early age, some things just are unlocked. And I think that you're able to think differently. And I'll give you a specific example of what I mean here. (00:12:51): He goes to Python class and he's coding. Now, I don't actually think he's going to have to code when he grows up. I think that's going to be a solved problem. But it's a very valuable skill because I think learning to program is learning how to think in a structured way, in a systematic way. And he was prompting ChatGPT with some really crazy things that I never even thought of. And one of the things was, "Hey, ChatGPT, can you give me a sentence that has every letter in the alphabet along the theme of oceans or along the theme of space?" (00:13:32): And the reason this kind of blew my mind is because in traditional programming you couldn't write that program. You can't say in Python like, "Oh, write a function that goes and formulate." I mean, it's a really difficult function to write. But for him to be able to think of that prompt, which is really cool because he built a custom GPT that you can type in any topic and it would give you a sentence that had every letter of the English alphabet, kind of like the quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog. Isn't that mind-blowing? (00:14:08): At age nine he could think about that, whereas being at age nine, I was playing with Legos and maybe QBasic. And so this idea of how young human's brains will evolve because of this new tool we have is going to change the way I think we're going to do education. And I'll be very honest, I'm not an expert in education, but I just thought a lot about it. And one thing I think is going to be really important in the future is being able to figure out how to ask the right questions. We humans are inherently inquisitive. But being inquisitive and turning that into the right questions to prompt or ask AI, which is going to be again, something that everyone's going to have access to is going to be a differentiator for what kind of work can be done. (00:14:56): The analogy I'll draw is, when the calculator was invented people didn't stop doing Math, they just did higher level Math. And it frees the mind up to do other things and think more at a higher level of abstraction. And I think we got to prepare our kids on thinking about, "Well, how do you think at a higher level of abstraction?" And this has happened before. I think Google has made memory kind of obsolete. You don't have to memorize facts anymore, you can just Google it. And the next phase will be something around, "Well code will just appear if you summon it." So, what are the things that people will think about and the skills we have to develop that are at the next level of abstraction, that tap into our creativity, that tap into our curiosity? That's going to be really interesting. So, I think education is going to change dramatically, just like how progressive education in the past switch from memorization of multiplication tables into something that's a little bit more kind of higher level, higher level thinking. And I think that's going to be one of those big areas.
turns.zh: 我觉得教育会发生巨大改变。我想了很多，因为我相当深度地参与了我孩子的学校——这是我离开 OpenAI 后在做的事。让我着迷的是，看着我儿子在那些 OpenAI 功能公开发布前就提前试用（我想我可以负责任地说，那看起来没问题）。当他玩 ChatGPT 和一些最新模型时，他当时才九岁，我已经能看到他的大脑在重新连接。他就开始提问了——他之前从没听过"prompt（提示词）"这个词，但就像人类心智如此奇妙，因为他很小就接触到这项技术，有些东西就被解锁了。我觉得你就能用不同的方式思考了。我给你一个具体的例子。(00:12:51): 他去上 Python 课，在写代码。现在，我其实不觉得他长大后就还需要写代码。我觉得那会是个被解决的问题。但这是项很有价值的技能，因为我认为学编程，就是学用结构化、系统化的方式思考。而他给 ChatGPT 的提示，有些疯狂到我从来没想过。其中之一是："嘿，ChatGPT，能不能给我一句包含字母表每个字母的话，主题是海洋，或者主题是太空？"(00:13:32): 这让我震惊的原因是，在传统编程里你写不出那个程序。你没法在 Python 里说"哦，写个函数去生成……"我是说，那是个很难写的函数。但他能想到那个提示，真的很酷，因为他做了一个自定义 GPT：你输入任意主题，它就能给你一句包含英文字母表每个字母的话，有点像"the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog（敏捷的棕狐跳过懒狗）"。这难道不让人震惊吗？(00:14:08): 九岁的他就能想到这个，而我九岁时在玩乐高，也许还有 QBasic。所以，年轻人的大脑因为这新工具而如何进化，将改变我们做教育的方式。老实说，我不是教育专家，但我确实想了很多。我觉得未来很重要的一点是，要学会如何提出正确的问题。人类天生好奇。但把好奇心转化成向 AI 提问或发出提示的正确问题——而 AI 人人都能用上——将成为能完成什么工作的分水岭。(00:14:56): 我打个比方：计算器被发明时，人们没有停止学数学，只是去学了更高阶的数学。它解放了心智去做别的事、在更高的抽象层上思考。我觉得我们得让孩子准备好思考"怎样在更高的抽象层上思考？"这种事以前也发生过。我认为 Google 让记忆变得有些过时了。你不必再死记事实，直接 Google 就行。下一阶段会是"你一召唤，代码就出现"。那么人们会去思考什么、我们必须培养的技能是什么——是那些更高抽象层的、能激发创造力和好奇心的东西？那会非常有趣。所以我认为教育会剧烈改变，就像过去进步主义教育从背诵乘法表转向了更高层、更高阶的思考。我觉得那会是重大领域之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This makes me think about an NPR story I was just listening to where they were following professors using ChatGPT to create their curriculum. There was a lot of talk of students using ChatGPT, cheating, having ChatGPT write their essays. But teachers are using ChatGPT in a big way. And then students are raiding professors badly because they noticed they're using ChatGPT for their curriculum. So, it's kind of this arms race.
turns.zh: 这让我想起刚听的一档 NPR 报道，他们追踪了一些用 ChatGPT 来设计课程的教授。关于学生用 ChatGPT、作弊、让 ChatGPT 写论文的讨论很多。但老师们也在大量使用 ChatGPT。然后学生们很不爽地发现教授们用 ChatGPT 设计课程。所以这有点像一场军备竞赛。

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: But it's also interesting because then that it goes further, it show further though. The whole system has to change. Because again, I still believe that human brains are inherently inquisitive and that we still need development in some way. But how that's going to develop, I'm fascinated to watch how that plays out.
turns.zh: 但这也很有意思，因为再往下想，整套系统都得变。因为 again，我仍然相信人类大脑天生好奇，我们仍需要某种方式去发展。但那会如何发展，我很有兴趣看它如何展开。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to get back to product, but first of all, I know something that you think a lot about along these lines. This came up in many conversations I had with folks that you worked with. Is your emphasis on the power and importance of language, being really good at thinking about the words you use both in writing and speaking. Just talk about how you think about that, just the importance and power of language as a leader.
turns.zh: 我想回到产品上，但首先，我知道有一件你沿这条线想了很多的事。这在我和你共事过的人聊的很多对话里都出现了。那就是你对语言的威力和重要性格外强调——无论是书面还是口头，都极善于斟酌自己用的词。就聊聊你是怎么看待这件事的，作为领导者，语言的重要性和力量。

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: I remember taking this class that really stuck with me in college. It was called Language and Thought. And it was taught by Herbert Clark. And he had this thesis that kind of blew my mind, which is that, "Language actually affects the way you think." That's one of the parts of the thesis. And once I heard that and read that in his book and listened to the lecture, I couldn't stop thinking about that because it just rang so true. I grew up speaking Chinese and I think that there's a lot of things of just the Chinese language that I feel like I noticed, I thought differently when I learned English. And there were some studies around this too, I think that there's, I think in, I'm not sure exactly, I just have to go check up on this. But I think in Russian there are two different words for blue, there's a greenish blue and a bright blue or something.
turns.zh: 我记得大学里上了一门让我印象极深的课，叫《语言与思维》（Language and Thought），是 Herbert Clark 教的。他有个让我震惊的论点："语言实际上会影响你的思维方式。"那是他论点的一部分。当我听到、读到此、又听了讲座后，就停不下来地想这件事，因为它太对了。我是说中文长大的，我觉得中文里有很多东西让我注意到——学了英文后我的思维方式变了。这方面也有一些研究，我想……具体我不太确定，得去查证。但我觉得俄语里"蓝"有两个不同的词，一种偏绿的蓝，一种明亮的蓝，之类的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I speak Russian but it's like... I moved to the U.S. when I was 6 and so my Russian is not great. So, I'm trying to think of this as you say it, but keep going.
turns.zh: 我会说俄语，但是……我 6 岁搬来美国，所以俄语不怎么样。所以我在努力边听边想你说的是什么，你继续。

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: Well, so then this is great. So, I need to get a way to validate this. But from what I remember, because there were these two different words for these different shades of blue Russian speakers who then learned English had an easier time distinguishing between these two shades of blue than, and a faster time doing so than people who had just grown up speaking English. So, I read some studies over there. And also there's some other languages that don't actually have a word for blue, I think. And then that's actually really hard for them to distinguish over time. So, that really stuck with me and I think that it's kind of rings true. So, when I, how I put it in practice, is that when I make slide decks, I gave a presentation to a class a couple of weeks ago and there were probably a total of 20 words on the entire slide deck. (00:19:07): And I spent hours obsessing over them because I really wanted to make sure I captured the right essence of what I was trying to say. And I think that crafting is really important when you're working in product, because if you're sitting down and you're writing a vision doc or you're writing a PRD, and if you don't pay attention to the words you use, and you're not intentional about it, those have downstream effects. People might misinterpret things, the connotations may not actually come through. And so I really am very careful about it because I think that there's a multiplicative effect and a downstream effect for using the wrong word. And I really believe in that kind of language affecting thought thesis which is why I've just really, really paid attention to that.
turns.zh: 好，那这很好。所以我得找个办法验证这一点。但根据我的记忆，因为有这两个表示不同蓝色深浅的词，那些先说俄语、后学英语的人，比只说英语长大的人，更容易、也更快区分这两种蓝。所以我读了些研究。而且有些语言里其实根本没有"蓝"这个词，我觉得。那对他们来说，久而久之要区分就真的很难。所以这点让我印象很深，我觉得它确实说得通。那我怎么把它用在实践中呢？我做幻灯片时——几周前我给一个班做演示，整个幻灯片大概总共只有 20 个词。(00:19:07): 我却花了好几个小时反复推敲这些词，因为我真的很想确保抓住了我想表达的核心。我觉得在产品工作中，措辞非常重要，因为当你坐下来写愿景文档或 PRD，如果不留意你用的词、不刻意而为，就会有下游影响。人们可能误读，那些言外之意可能传达不出来。所以我非常小心，因为我认为用错一个词会有乘数效应和连锁的下游影响。我真的很相信"语言影响思维"这个论点，这也是为什么我一直、一直非常看重它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm. Yeah. And I feel like AI can help you with that too.
turns.zh: 嗯。对。而且我觉得 AI 也能帮你做这个。

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: Yes. Exactly.
turns.zh: 是的。正是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We had an episode-
turns.zh: 我们有一期节目——

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: Well, actually, speaking of AI, actually that's a really interesting point. I think it's really interesting and kind of poetic and fitting that the breakthrough in artificial intelligence came from large language models. It's interesting to me because there is, with every word in every sentence so much of the knowledge is encapsulated and shaped. And when ChatGPT does something really interesting, I tell people it's oftentimes just writing Python code and interpreting it. And Python is a language yet again. So, I think that there's something really interesting where like the condensation of human thought in language is related to the LLMs and the advancement scenario that we have today.
turns.zh: 其实，说到 AI，这真的是个很有意思的点。我觉得人工智能的突破来自大语言模型，既有趣又颇具诗意和契合感。让我感兴趣的是，每个句子里的每个词，都浓缩并塑造了如此多的知识。当 ChatGPT 做了件很有趣的事，我常跟人说，它往往只是在写 Python 代码并解读它。而 Python 又是一种语言。所以我觉得有件很有意思的事：人类思想在语言中的凝结，与今天的 LLM 和进步是相关的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think it was Ilya on a Dwarkesh's podcast where he was talking about, you may think LLMs are just like, "Oh, just predicting the next word, what's the big deal?" But in order to do that, it has to understand the universe and everything in the world that has ever happened and existed and everything anyone's ever written to predict the next word.
turns.zh: 我想是 Ilya 在 Dwarkesh 的播客上说的，大意是，你也许觉得 LLM 不过是"哦，就预测下一个词，有什么大不了？"但为了做到这点，它必须理解这个宇宙、世界上发生过和存在过的一切、以及任何人写过的一切，才能预测下一个词。

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: Yeah, love it.
turns.zh: 对，爱了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Okay. So, let me zoom out a little bit and shift a little bit to just product in general.
turns.zh: 对。好。那么让我稍微退一步，转到产品这个更宏观的话题。

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You've worked at and built some of those iconic products in history. You worked at OpenAI, Facebook, Uber a Head of Product at Instagram. So, let me just ask you this question and see where this goes. What's the most counterintuitive lesson you've learned about building products or leading teams that goes against common wisdom?
turns.zh: 你曾参与打造历史上一些标志性的产品。你在 OpenAI、Facebook、Uber 工作过，还是 Instagram 的产品负责人。那我就直接问这个问题，看聊到哪：关于打造产品或领导团队，你学到的最反直觉、最违背常识的一课是什么？

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: I think one thing that, it's a really hard lesson that I learned at Uber, which is sometimes your product actually doesn't matter. And by product I mean the pixels you put on the screen or things that you build in your mobile app. And at Uber, I learned this because, it pains me to say this, but really the price and the ETA at Uber was the product. And I think a lot of times people at tech companies think of the product as just this digital manifestation, but looking at it from a holistic perspective, we humans consume the entirety of the product. And I think that was one of the things that I learned, the lessons that I learned that was really kind of hard hitting, that sometimes the pixels don't matter as much as you think. And you fix a certain bug, it's not to say that you shouldn't fix the bug, but it doesn't have as much of an impact as something that is more important to people like a price or ETA. (00:22:29): And this happens a lot in B2B products where it's not just about how... It's great that your product is well-loved by its end users, but does it make good business sense? Is one of those hard lessons I learned as a very bright-eyed, bushy tailed sort of design-based product manager going into Uber. I think the other insight that I had or other thought I had the other day was just the idea that so many of the tech companies today, this is kind of counterintuitive, so many of the tech companies that are most valuable today didn't really start with any technological breakthrough. They were built on some kind of technological breakthrough and they ended up building a lot more technology. But really a lot of these companies, like Facebook for example, just put in the hard work, the elbow grease, especially in the early stages, to take essentially a database of human connections and build something valuable on top of it. (00:23:31): And that keep on polishing and iterating that product and coming up with new ones like newsfeed and photo tagging just kind of came out of just really paying attention to what people wanted. And some of the ideas are super simple and it's not something that came out of the lab. So, Uber for example, took the fact that everyone had these GPS devices in their pockets, and they didn't invent the GPS device, but they were able to take that and the fact that people had cars, and people wanted to get around, and there was a human need, and they just connected the dots, and put everything together. (00:24:11): And eventually, built a ton of tech to predict the right marketplace and pricing et cetera. But largely that's a very valuable tech company. But it's largely an operations company. And I want to give a huge shout-out to my colleagues there who run Uber Eats and Uber Rides from operations perspective. Because truly that was one of the biggest business model hacks that I've seen. And so I think that it's Silicon Valley it gets lost a lot. It's like, "Oh, this is a new tech company." Oftentimes some of the most valuable ones are just the ones that are just building what people need on top of existing tech.
turns.zh: 我觉得有件事——是我在 Uber 学到的一堂很痛的课——有时候你的产品其实根本不重要。我说的"产品"，是指你放在屏幕上的那些像素，或你在移动 App 里构建的东西。在 Uber，我学到这点，因为说这话让我心痛，但 Uber 真正重要的产品是价格和 ETA。我觉得科技公司的很多人把产品想成只是那种数字化的呈现，但从整体角度看，我们人类消费的是产品的全部。那是我学到、也让我深受触动的一课：有时候像素没你想的那么重要。你修了个 bug，并不是说你不该修，但它带来的影响，不如价格或 ETA 这类对用户更重要的事情。(00:22:29): 这在 B2B 产品里很常见——你的产品深受终端用户喜爱当然很好，但它有商业意义吗？这是我作为初出茅庐、满腔热忱、偏设计导向的产品经理进 Uber 时学到的一堂硬课。另一点我前些天想到的洞察是：今天这么多最有价值的科技公司，这有点反直觉——它们其实并非从某种技术突破起步。它们建立在某种技术突破之上，后来又建了很多技术。但很多这类公司，比如 Facebook，靠的只是苦功夫、实打实的努力，尤其早期，去把本质上一个"人类关系数据库"变得有价值，并在其上构建东西。(00:23:31): 然后不断打磨、迭代那个产品，又搞出 newsfeed、照片标记这种新东西，其实就来自认真关注人们想要什么。有些点子特别简单，不是实验室里出来的。比如 Uber，利用的是人人口袋里都有 GPS 设备这个事实——他们没发明 GPS，但他们把这一点、加上人们有车、人们想出行、存在着人的需求，连点成线，拼到了一起。(00:24:11): 最终他们建了大量技术来预测正确的市场和定价等等。但它本质上是一家很有价值的科技公司，却也是一家运营公司。我要向那边负责 Uber Eats 和 Uber Rides 运营的同事们致以巨大敬意。因为说真的，那是我见过最大的商业模式"黑客"之一。所以我觉得硅谷常常迷失在这点上，总说"哦，这是家新科技公司"。但往往最有价值的那些，不过是在现有技术之上，构建人们需要的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's so much to say here. I love it. And this is coming from someone that led the Uber Rider product team and worked at Facebook and a Head of Product at Instagram. It means a lot coming from someone like you, not someone that's not in product especially.
turns.zh: 可说的太多了。我喜欢。而且这番话出自一个领导过 Uber 乘客端产品团队、在 Facebook 工作过、又当过 Instagram 产品负责人之手。从你这样的人嘴里说出来分量很重，尤其不是一个不在产品圈的人说的。

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, just to go further on the Instagram part, the idea was super simple. It was showing photos and visual sharing. But the craft that Mike and Kevin had in putting in the hard work to get the product just right, that's what made it really take off. That's a great example. I had forgotten about Instagram, but how could I? But it wasn't anything that any other company couldn't have done, but it was that product taste that Kevin and Mike had and conviction that there's a certain sort of vibe, if you will, that people wanted, and building that and iterating, and look at it now, it's a core part of our lives. Visual sharing, they really solved it.
turns.zh: 对，我是说，再往 Instagram 那块说，点子特别简单，就是展示照片和视觉分享。但 Mike 和 Kevin 在打磨产品、下苦功把产品做到位这件事上的匠心，才是让它真正起飞的原因。那是个好例子。我差点忘了 Instagram，但我怎么会忘呢？其实别的公司也能做，但 Kevin 和 Mike 那种产品品味和信念——他们认为人们想要某种氛围（如果你愿意这么说）——去构建它、迭代它，看看现在，它成了我们生活的核心部分。视觉分享，他们真的解决了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I just had Mike Krieger on the podcast. So, it's interesting, there's two tensions here. One is just the product doesn't matter in a lot of really successful companies. It's secondary to the cars, the drivers, the GPS and the phone. And then on the other hand, there doesn't need to be a technological breakthrough to build a huge business. It's almost like if there's no technological breakthrough, then the product matters. Facebook is an example. Basically, it's like a database of connections, but what allowed an Instagram, what allowed them to breakthrough, and there's classically competitors at the time. Was the experience, was it a lot better? And then maybe on the flip side, if the experience doesn't matter, then it's the breakthrough is on the operations and other... Does that resonate? Is that kind of what you're saying?
turns.zh: 对，我刚请了 Mike Krieger 上播客。所以有意思的是，这里有两股张力。一是，在很多非常成功的公司里，产品根本不重要。它次于车、司机、GPS 和手机。而另一方面，做大生意并不需要技术突破。这几乎像是：如果没有技术突破，那产品才重要。Facebook 就是个例子。基本上它就像一个关系数据库，但让 Instagram 得以突破的——当时经典地存在竞争者——是体验，是它好得多吗？也许反过来说，如果体验不重要，那突破就在于运营和其他……这和你说的共鸣吗？大致是你想表达的意思？

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: It does resonate. I think both have to be true. But also I would say that even if you did found a company that has a huge technological breakthrough. Very shortly, I think that the product experience will start mattering, because how long does that technological advantage last before humans wisen up to be like, "Well, this is not the product I want to use. I use it a little bit differently and this is more ergonomic for me?" Et cetera. So, I think that what you said is a beautiful summary. I also think that a point in time in a company's history will also determine what is going to be more important.
turns.zh: 是共鸣的。我觉得两者都得成立。但我也想说，即便你创办了一家有巨大技术突破的公司，很快，产品体验就会开始变得重要，因为那项技术优势能维持多久，人类就会反应过来："嗯，这不是我想用的产品。我用它的方式略有不同，这个对我更顺手？"等等。所以我觉得你说的总结很漂亮。我也认为，公司发展史上的某个时点，也会决定什么更重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is, especially, interesting for companies building on top of LLMs and AI infrastructure, where you're essentially saying, you don't need to have some kind of technological breakthrough to build something valuable if you can create a really special, unique experience that unlocks the potential of this super intelligence.
turns.zh: 这对建立在 LLM 和 AI 基础设施之上的公司尤其有意思——你基本上是在说，如果你能创造一种真正特别、独特的体验，解锁这种超级智能的潜力，你不需要什么技术突破也能做出有价值的东西。

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: I think that's right. And I have some more thoughts on just sort of the companies that are building on top of LLMs that are just... That's a slightly different thing I would say. I think that for them, having the right data, and that right data flywheel's is so important.
turns.zh: 我想这是对的。关于那些建立在 LLM 之上的公司，我还有些想法……那是略有不同的一件事。我觉得对它们来说，拥有正确的数据，以及那个正确的数据飞轮，太重要了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Like proprietary data especially.
turns.zh: 尤其是专有数据。

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: Exactly. And the flywheel part is just, you can start with proprietary data, but the flywheel is really just sort of how do you continue to maintain that and generate that. And the second thing is, again, it's the workflow. So, it's the ergonomics of how does it actually integrate into people's lives? And that is going to be more and more important.
turns.zh: 没错。而飞轮这部分就是，你可以从专有数据起步，但飞轮真正关乎的是你如何持续维持并生成它。第二件事 again，是工作流。也就是它如何真正融入人们的生活——那种"人体工学"式的契合。那会越来越重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, let's actually spend more time there because a lot of people are thinking about this. It feels like everybody's trying to start a company these days with AI enabling so much more. And so I think a lot of people are just curious, where should they spend time? And so I think this is actually really interesting. So, what I'm hearing here is two things to think about to create any kind of moat, defensibility against, say, foundational models coming to your lunch or in other companies. What sort of data can you acquire that is proprietary and create a flywheel to generate more of that data? And then the other piece is how do you fit into a very specific, basically, vertical that you understand really well that fits into their existing workflow? Is that...? I'm probably right.
turns.zh: 好，我们其实多花点时间在这上面，因为很多人在想这个。现在感觉人人都想趁 AI 让太多事变可能而去创业。所以我觉得很多人好奇：他们该把时间花在哪？我觉得这真的很有意思。所以我听到的是，要构建任何护城河、对任何防御性（比如基础模型来抢你的午餐，或其他公司），要思考两件事：你能获取什么专有数据，并创造一个飞轮来生成更多这样的数据？另一块是，你如何切入一个你非常了解的、非常具体的垂直领域，融入他们现有的工作流？是吗？我大概说对了。

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: Yeah. Well, it's, again, this is something we can unpack for a long time. Because with any product that you want to build, there's going to be incumbents that have distribution advantages. But I do have this thesis that there are certain-
turns.zh: 对。嗯，again，这事我们可以拆很久。因为任何你想做的产品，都会有占据分发优势的老玩家。但我有个论点是，有些——

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: ... have distribution advantages, but I do have this thesis that there are certain products that will be able to break through those advantages of the distribution of the other companies, but you have to overcome a pretty high bar of your product has to be so much better. I think that's one thing. (00:29:18): But yeah, I think that data flywheel thing is really interesting because the models will get really good at whatever data you show it, and that's one of the things that people just think that AI is such a magic wand. But no, it's like if it's been trained on the right data, it's going to do the thing that it's been trained on. It's very malleable. (00:29:36): Being very mindful of the data that you have access to to start your flywheel going and what you can do to keep on going with that flywheel is going to be a critical thing for anyone who's starting a company today.
turns.zh: ……有分发优势，但我有个论点是，有些产品能突破那些公司的分发优势，但你必须跨过一个相当高的门槛：你的产品必须好太多。我觉得这是一点。(00:29:18): 不过对，我觉得数据飞轮这事很有意思，因为模型在你喂给它的任何数据上都会变得很好——这是人们以为 AI 是根魔杖的地方。但不是，就像如果它在正确的数据上训练过，它就会做它受训去做的事。它非常可塑。(00:29:36): 非常清楚你起步飞轮能用上什么数据、以及你如何让它持续转下去，对今天任何创业的人都是关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's make that even more specific. When you talk about this, I think about... The CEO of Windsurf was on the podcast and we talked a lot about how they've all this really unique data about which recommendations of code snippets people accept and reject and they actually launched their model I think based on that. Is that example? Any other examples to make this real?
turns.zh: 让我们说得更具体些。你聊这个时，我想到……Windsurf 的 CEO 上过播客，我们聊了很多他们如何拥有关于"人们接受和拒绝哪些代码片段推荐"的独特数据，我觉得他们其实就是基于那个推出了自己的模型。这是例子吗？还有其他例子让它更真实吗？

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: That's a perfect example. (00:30:10): There's some companies I've invested in that aren't public yet that have their own take on that, which is really interesting to be able to take whatever activity is in their product to get smarter at the thing that they are doing, again, which is why I think the data flywheel and the workflow goes so hand in hand together, because if you are solving something actually valuable for businesses, for people, and there's a lot of that attention that's being paid to, a lot of work is being done through it, you're going to have that edge. (00:30:45): This is where I see again startups in very different markets who have this insight, who understand this very deeply, and are not just trying to zero shot everything and be like, "No, no, no. This is how we're going to build it to make the product genuinely useful so that it can get genuinely more useful over time." (00:31:02): That is going to be amazing because as a consumer of any of these products, we're going to benefit.
turns.zh: 那是个完美的例子。(00:30:10): 我投了一些还没公开的公司，它们有自己的玩法，挺有意思——能利用产品里的任何活动让自己在所做的这件事上更聪明。again，这也是为什么我觉得数据飞轮和工作流如此密不可分，因为如果你在为企业、为人真正解决有价值的事，有很多注意力投在上面、很多工作通过它完成，你就会拥有那种优势。(00:30:45): 这正是我看到的一些身处完全不同市场、却有这番洞察、理解极深的初创公司，它们不只是想靠零样本（zero shot）搞定一切、说"不不不，我们就是要这样构建，让产品真正有用，从而随时间真正变得更有用"。(00:31:02): 那会非常棒，因为任何用这些产品的人，我们都会受益。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I'm hearing here is also if you don't have proprietary data or unique data, you can still have a chance by building this flywheel where you collect that data through your usage. (00:31:18): For example, Windsurf, if they all built on Claude 3.5 and then now they have all this unique data and now they're launching their models.
turns.zh: 我听到的还有一点：如果你没有专有数据或独特数据，你仍可以通过构建这个飞轮——通过你的使用去收集那些数据——来拥有机会。(00:31:18): 比如 Windsurf，如果他们全都建立在 Claude 3.5 之上，现在他们有了这些独特数据，就推出了自己的模型。

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: That's exactly right. (00:31:26): This goes back to something I might've mentioned briefly, but you got to have grit when you're building anything. You got to be able to have that vision, have that clear direction, and be able to really go chase that. I think that's really important.
turns.zh: 完全正确。(00:31:26): 这回到我可能简单提过的一点：做任何事你都得有韧性（grit）。你得有那个愿景、那个清晰的方向，并真正去追逐它。我觉得那非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To make your example of distribution being overcomable, a great example I think a lot about, and we had CPO, turns out there's many CPOs at Microsoft, I didn't realize how many CPOs they had, and I asked her about, "Why didn't Copilot..." The fastest growing companies in the world, Cursor, Windsurf, Lovable, Bolt, all these guys. Copilot was so ahead of these companies and these companies broke through. (00:32:05): While Microsoft has distribution, amazing talent, infrastructure, all the things, early first mover advantage and it's to your point, they were just building products that were much better, Cursor, Windsurf, all these, Lovable, Bolt.
turns.zh: 要说明"分发优势是可以被克服的"，我想了很多的一个好例子——我们聊过 Microsoft 的 CPO（结果发现他们有好多 CPO，我没想到他们有那么多），我问她"为什么 Copilot 没有……"世界上增长最快的公司，Cursor、Windsurf、Lovable、Bolt，所有这些。Copilot 比这些公司领先那么多，而这些公司却突破了。(00:32:05): 尽管 Microsoft 有分发、惊人人才、基础设施、所有东西、早期先发优势，但正如你所说，这些公司（Cursor、Windsurf、Lovable、Bolt）只是把产品做得好太多了。

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: I do believe there is a level of product craft that will make it so that it's just worth it to switch or try something else. There are a few products out there that I see with this. I think Granola is one of them. (00:32:31): There's so many distribution advantages that Google Meet has, that Google, Facebook started off, Microsoft Teams has, Zoom has, but they're just these tiny little product craft delightful things that I really appreciate myself of like, "Yeah, they got it." (00:32:50): They have these little edges, set it down just right, and they've really figured out a way to really make it so delightful that it's like, "Yeah, I will install this piece of software. Yes, 100% I will talk to my friends about this because it is so life-changing." (00:33:08): We're starting to see that now. Again, before, I would say 18 months ago, it's like, "Oh, well, who has the best model?" But then coming forward, it's like really who has the best workflow and who has the best product, and we humans are just demanding. We want the best. And so when someone is going to come out and produce something that's so well-crafted, I think people are going to pay attention.
turns.zh: 我确实相信，存在一种产品匠心，会让"切换或尝试别的东西"变得值得。我看到几款这样的产品。我觉得 Granola 是其中之一。(00:32:31): Google Meet 有那么多分发优势，Google 起步时有、Facebook 有、Microsoft Teams 有、Zoom 有，但它们就是有一些微小却令人愉悦的产品匠心细节，我自己真的很欣赏，像是"对，他们懂了"。(00:32:50): 它们有这些小优势，恰到好处地落地，真的找到了一种方法让人觉得"对，我会装这个软件。会，百分之百我会跟朋友聊它，因为它太改变生活了"。(00:33:08): 我们开始看到这个了。Again，以前，我会说 18 个月前，是"哦，谁有最好的模型？"但现在往前看，是"到底谁有最好的工作流、谁有最好的产品"，而我们人类就是苛求，我们要最好的。所以当有人做出如此精雕细琢的东西，我觉得人们会注意到的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A couple of takeaways here is if you're trying to build an AI startup, a few things you should be thinking about that gives you a better chance of breaking through and winning is what are your data flywheels where you collect proprietary unique data, how do you build something the craft comes through and people are wowed and want to tell their friends about it. (00:33:47): Granola is a great example. Clearly, Cursor, Lovable, Bolt, Rep, all these guys did that and then it feels like they just understand a vertical workflow really well and someone's problem and solve that in a really unique way.
turns.zh: 这里几个要点是：如果你想做 AI 创业，提高突破和取胜几率要想的几件事——你的数据飞轮在哪、能收集专有独特数据；你如何做出匠心透出来、让人惊艳、想告诉朋友的产品。(00:33:47): Granola 是好例子。显然，Cursor、Lovable、Bolt、Rep，所有这些人都做到了，然后感觉他们就是极其理解某个垂直工作流、理解某人的问题，并以非常独特的方式去解决。

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: Yeah. I couldn't have put it better myself.
turns.zh: 对。我自己没法说得更好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. (00:34:02): Let me ask you, this came up in my chat with Mike at Anthropic and it's along these lines. I was thinking about just what is product doing at Anthropic. (00:34:10): They're building this basically a gigabrain super intelligence thing that's going to know everything and maybe build its own experience in the future. And then there's this product team building this layer on top to interact with this super intelligence gigabrain.
turns.zh: 太棒了。(00:34:02): 我问你这个，它来自我和 Anthropic 的 Mike 的聊天，是沿这条线的。我在想 Anthropic 的产品到底在做什么。(00:34:10): 他们在打造基本上一个"千兆大脑"超级智能，未来会知道一切、也许会自己构建体验。然后有个产品团队在它之上构建一层，来与这个超级智能千兆大脑交互。

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: What is the point? What is the value of that layer?
turns.zh: 那有什么意义？那一层价值何在？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You spoke to it a bit here of just there's value in the experience and feeling native, but I guess let me just ask you that. Just where do you think product goes at a company like Anthropic, OpenAI where there's just the super intelligence that the team is working on and there's this UX on top?
turns.zh: 你这里提到一点，就是"体验感、原生感"有价值，但我想直接问你。你觉得在 Anthropic、OpenAI 这类公司，产品会走向何方——既有团队在做那个超级智能，又有 UX 层在上面？

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: I think those companies have just such an advantage because you get to work in the same building as the researchers. I think that there's that really symbiotic relationship, close partnership between post training and product where, again, more and more it's going to be less about the raw intelligence, it's going to be about the fine tuning of what the model can do that really resonates with people and what people want and also what the product trajectory is going to be. I think that you're going to see that more and more. (00:35:15): I think this is less about Anthropic but more about OpenAI. I think OpenAI made a great move. (00:35:21): I am a huge Fidji fan. As soon as that news leaked that she was going to join, I texted her. I was like, "This is great. Amazing. Congratulations." (00:35:29): I'm thrilled for her, for the company, for all of my friends still at OpenAI because it's just going to be this amazing leader coming in. (00:35:36): I'm also thrilled as a consumer because some great products are going to come out. (00:35:39): I think really that close, tight-knit relationship at any of these large model companies between post training and product is going to produce some really incredible stuff.
turns.zh: 我觉得那些公司有巨大的优势，因为你能在同一栋楼里和研究员一起工作。我觉得后训练（post training）和产品之间有种真正的共生关系、紧密合作，而 again，越来越不是比原始智能，而是比模型能做什么的微调——那真正能与人和人的需求共振、以及产品的走向。(00:35:15): 我觉得这更少关于 Anthropic，更多关于 OpenAI。我觉得 OpenAI 走了一步好棋。(00:35:21): 我是 Fidji 的超级粉丝。那消息一泄露说她要加入，我就给她发了短信，说"这太棒了。厉害。恭喜"。(00:35:29): 我为她、为公司、为我所有还在 OpenAI 的朋友感到激动，因为会有一位超棒的领导者加入。(00:35:36): 作为用户我也很激动，因为会出一些很棒的产品。(00:35:39): 我觉得在任何大模型公司，后训练和产品之间那种紧密、团结的关系，都会产出一些真正不可思议的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First of all, Mike actually said very similar things that the more-
turns.zh: 首先，Mike 其实说过非常类似的话——越——

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: I promise you I did not watch that podcast.
turns.zh: 我向你保证我没看那期播客。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It hasn't even come out yet so I believe you. (00:35:59): Yeah. He had this interesting finding where he put product people on UX product experience front-facing product and then he put PMs on the research teams and building models, helping models get better, helping researchers build things, and he found that all the leverage and wins came from the PMs working with the researchers, much less so on the product experience. And so he puts more and more PMs with that team.
turns.zh: 它还没播出来呢，所以我信你。(00:35:59): 对。他有个有趣的发现：他把产品人放在 UX 产品体验、面向用户的产品上，又把 PM 放在研究团队、做模型、帮模型变好、帮研究员构建东西，然后他发现所有的杠杆和胜利都来自 PM 和研究员一起工作，在产品体验上少得多。所以他把越来越多 PM 放到那个团队。

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: I'm so thrilled to hear that because that's a little bit... It's very validating because that's what we did at OpenAI too. We were very closely tied to the post training team and it was because of that tight collaboration that you see some of the advances of ChatGPT getting better at so many things. It's great. It's awesome that we independently came to the same conclusion.
turns.zh: 听到这个我太高兴了，因为这有点……非常印证，因为我们在 OpenAI 也是这么做的。我们和后期训练团队绑得很紧，正是那种紧密协作，让你看到 ChatGPT 在很多事上变得更好。很好。我们独立得出了相同结论，真棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes. It's a good sign. (00:36:46): Okay, so we're talking about startups, building new companies. I want to follow this thread a little bit.
turns.zh: 对。是个好兆头。(00:36:46): 好，我们聊创业、建新公司。我想顺着这条线再走一点。

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like you've built more products from zero to one to scale than maybe most anyone else across all the companies that you've worked at. I'm going to do a quick rundown of some of the things you've done and I'm going to miss a bunch but let's see. (00:37:06): You built and led the Facebook Newsfeed, the current version of it. You built the new groups experience chat and messages. You shipped the Messenger app as its own app. That was one of your projects. (00:37:16): You led UberPool low-cost rides. You launched ChatGPT Enterprise. You shipped voice and vision, memory, custom GPTs, just refreshing the whole design of ChatGPT. Many more things. (00:37:31): A lot of work at Airtable obviously. Also, Oculus. (00:37:35): These are just some examples in the intro. I'm going to try to go through all these things. (00:37:39): All that to say, I feel like you've seen a lot of what works and doesn't work, building from idea from zero essentially to one to scale. So let me just ask you this question, what's an important lesson you've learned about what it takes to succeed building something from idea to one to billions?
turns.zh: 我觉得你从零到一、再到规模化打造的产品，可能比几乎任何其他人都多，跨越你待过的所有公司。我快速过一遍你做过的一些事，肯定会漏掉很多，但我们看看。(00:37:06): 你打造并领导了 Facebook 现在的 Newsfeed 版本。你打造了全新的群组体验、聊天和消息。你把 Messenger 作为独立 App 发布。那是你的项目之一。(00:37:16): 你领导了 UberPool 低价乘车。你推出了 ChatGPT Enterprise。你发布了语音和视觉、记忆、自定义 GPT，只是刷新了 ChatGPT 的整个设计。还有更多。(00:37:31): Airtable 上当然很多工作。还有 Oculus。(00:37:35): 这些只是介绍里的一些例子。我会试着过完所有这些。(00:37:39): 说这么多，是想说我觉得你见过很多管用和不管用的事，从想法、从零、基本上到一、再到规模化。那我就直接问：关于从想法到一、再到数十亿规模做成一件事，你学到的重要一课是什么？

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: Yeah. Thank you. That was a good trip down memory lane too when you read that off. (00:38:04): I think the first thing I would say, going from zero to one is different going from one to 100. When you are in the one to 100 phase, which is a lot of the time that I spent is the one to 100 phase, we quadruple Instagram usage in two years, that was very much a fun ride and there's a bunch of other examples at other companies. (00:38:31): But when you go to one to 100, I think one of the things that you really got to take into account is that you have to plan your chess moves out in advance. You have to really think before you act and build systems that are going to let you go sustainably faster, because the zero to one is you're trying to find that product market fit and then when you get to one to 100, you're trying to make sure you can get to hyperscale as fast as you can. (00:38:59): I've been very fortunate to be along the ride of many of these products as they were going through that hyperscale. And the analogy I always like to use is that when you do that, you feel the G-forces. Some people are like, "Oh, yeah, I'm a pilot, I can fly at 35,000 feet." But feeling the G-forces of takeoff of a rocket is very different. (00:39:19): One thing that I've learned there doing that a few times is you got to build the systems that help you move sustainably faster, and sometimes, you have to go slow to go fast. (00:39:29): Here's an example. (00:39:31): In building the Newsfeed, the current version that we have today, it really hasn't changed much from the time that we built it, I don't even know, it was like 12 years ago or something, I don't know the reason why it hasn't changed much. (00:39:43): But I like to think that it's because we put a lot of time and craft into thinking about the whole sharing loop and what are the key pieces of it and how is it architected, what's the information architecture, and what does that whole flow look like, how does it go from posting something at the top of the page to showing up in the newsfeed to someone clicking like and then that notifications thing lighting up red and then that repeating over and over again. (00:40:11): I like to think that Newsfeed has stood the test of time, the current version of it, because we thought very carefully about how people wanted to interact and how people wanted to consume information and also, that whole loop. When that happens, then I think things are built to last. I think this is a case at a lot of different companies. (00:40:33): When I was at Uber, we had a bit of a spaghetti string code situation on the writer app, but taking a step back and re-architecting things of what are the core components and how do you actually make it so that the product selector can scale around the world. (00:40:48): Here's a little known fact. Talk about grit and elbow grease. (00:40:53): Uber's not just as simple as finding a ride. If you've ever been to another country, like in India, sometimes, there are no street signs, so you have to pick up in front of this mini mart or whatever it might be. There's a whole team that worked on pickup and drop-offs. This was a large effort. (00:41:08): It sounds so boring but it was so critical to Uber being able to scale because pickup and drop-offs team thought about, "Well, how do you do it for venues?" That venues and finding that right abstraction means that you can have a scalable way to do pickups at airports and configure different venues. (00:41:26): Those systems when you take the time to build them in the one to 100 phase help you speed up massively and that's how you get 4x users in two years. (00:41:37): Or on Messenger, we put a lot of thought into the infrastructure around push notifications, etc. We grew that product from zero to 4.7 billion messages sent per day in about two and a half years. I think it really requires that forethought in building the right systems.
turns.zh: 对。谢谢。你念出来的时候也让我好好回忆了一番。(00:38:04): 我觉得我要说的第一点是，从零到一，和从一到一百，是不同的。当你处于一到一百的阶段——我大量时间都在这个阶段——我们在两年里让 Instagram 使用量翻了两番，那是段很愉快的旅程，其他公司也有不少类似例子。(00:38:31): 但从一到一百时，你真要考虑的一件事是，你必须提前规划好棋步。你必须谋定而后动，并建立能让你持续加速的系统，因为零到一是你在找产品市场契合，而从一到一百时，你是想确保尽可能快地达到超大规模。(00:38:59): 我很幸运能随其中很多产品经历那种超大规模。我总喜欢用的类比是：做这事时，你能感受到 G 力。有些人说"哦对，我是飞行员，能在三万五千英尺飞"。但感受火箭起飞的 G 力，完全不同。(00:39:19): 我做这事儿几次学到的一点是，你得建立帮你持续更快前行的系统，有时候，你得——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me follow that thread real quickly because that's really interesting. (00:41:58): Essentially, what you're saying is there's a phase of once you find product market fit, and I want to actually ask you this before you start planning, when you're starting to scale going from one to a hundred, your advice here is basically don't move fast and break things. Don't ship MVPs. This is the time to really think many chess moves ahead about what you're going to need to get this to, say, a billion users.
turns.zh: 让我顺着这条线快速跟一下，因为很有意思。(00:41:58): 本质上，你的意思是，一旦找到产品市场契合，而在你开始规划之前我想先问你这个——当你开始从一到一百扩张，你的建议基本上是"别急着动、别把东西搞坏。别发 MVP。"现在是真正要多想几步棋、想清楚要够到比如十亿用户需要什么的时候。

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. It's building the systems and then that systems thinking will carry you really far, or at least that's been my experience and hopefully, you can find the same way but your biology may vary. But yeah, that's exactly right.
turns.zh: 对，对。是建立系统，然后那种系统思维会带你走很远——至少这是我的经验，希望你能找到同样的方式，不过因人而异。但对，正是如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's your guidance on just when to do that? Because you build something, okay, well it's working, there's also this just like, "Okay, let's just keep it going, let's scale it as far as we can." In your experience, is it... Just what's the guidance on when to really step back and really think years and years ahead?
turns.zh: 关于何时该这么做，你有什么指引？因为你做了个东西，嗯，它管用了，也有种"好，继续推，尽量规模化"的冲动。在你的经验里，是……关于何时真正退一步、想好几年甚至更远的未来，有什么指引？

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: Great question. (00:42:50): The first thing I'll say is that it's not a binary switch. It's actually a ramp rate. (00:42:56): When I've led teams, I've always believed strongly in this portfolio approach. Famously, Google had the 70-20-10 portfolio approach. That may be the right thing for a more mature company, maybe it's 50/50 if you're a startup, but you have to think about this in a non-binary way and in a way, that's about scaling up and when do you need to put more resources behind that. (00:43:20): Every startup is going to be different. Every product that you're launching is going to be different. And then thinking about your portfolio approach and how much you allocate your time that would be my advice. It's really dependent on the stage that you're in. (00:43:35): I think that actually is a nice dovetail to my second thing, if I may, which is when you're going from that stage of maybe one to five or one to 10, so not just fully one to 100, one thing I found to be very helpful is to measure everything. (00:43:54): This sounds, again, very simple but just like how you wouldn't fly a plane without instruments, why would you run your products without understanding the instrumentation and how it's doing. (00:44:06): One of the things I did in pretty much all the teams that I led, whether it was Instagram, Uber, Airtable, was all about... ChatGPT too. (00:44:15): One of the first things I did was always to build a growth team. (00:44:19): Building a growth team is really interesting because it actually is a simple razor, it's a simple thing to think about. It's like, "I'm going to build a growth team," but then you're going to uncover a lot of things. (00:44:29): You're going to uncover how much stuff you have not yet logged and how non-rigorous you've been looking at your entire product. (00:44:38): It's so funny because I've seen this movie so many times, the same movie so many times that every one of these companies where I remember walking into Instagram and I think asking Kevin and Mike, "So how many users do we have?" It's like, "Well, we don't really know." And so it's like, "Well, there are a lot and we don't really know." (00:44:56): When you build a growth team and you hire the right growth leader, I've had the pleasure of working with George Lee at Instagram, some of the early growth folks at Facebook, Andrew Chen at Uber, Airtable. I had the privilege of working with Lauryn, who is currently now leading growth at Notion. I've been very fortunate to work with some really amazing people on my team. (00:45:20): When you hire the right person, they start asking all the right questions because when the archetype of person who is a growth PM will be like, "Well, wait. Why is this happening? And let's get the data on X, Y and Z thing." That's when you realize you don't have X, Y, and Z thing logged and after you have X, Y, and Z thing logged, you look at the data, you're like, "Wait. Well, why is that happening?" And then you're forcing yourself to go deeper into the analysis of doing some analysis of like, "Well, what's correlated with what and what are some hypotheses?" (00:45:49): Because growth leaders, growth product leaders are so into this experimentation side, it actually is this really easy thing to do is when you start building a growth team, it just begets all of the right questions being asked and then it starts turning into all the right behaviors of taking something you've been building, which seems like it's working into a more rigorous system. (00:46:12): That's zero, sorry, the one to 10 phase I would say that really sets you up for the 10 to 100.
turns.zh: 好问题。(00:42:50): 我要说的第一点是，这不是一个二元的开关，它其实是一个爬升速率（ramp rate）。(00:42:56): 我带团队时，一直强烈相信这种组合（portfolio）式思路。 famously，Google 有 70-20-10 的组合式思路。对更成熟的公司那也许对，如果你是初创，也许是 50/50，但你必须用非二元的方式想这个问题，以一种关于上规模、以及何时需要在那上面投更多资源的方式。(00:43:20): 每家初创都不同。你推出的每个产品都不同。然后思考你的组合式思路、你分配多少时间，那会是我的建议。真取决于你所处的阶段。(00:43:35): 我觉得这其实能很自然地接到我的第二点，如果可以——当你从也许一到五、或一到十的阶段，而不只是完全的一到一百，我发现非常有用的一点是：度量一切。(00:43:54): 这 again 听起来很简单，但就像你不会不靠仪表开飞机，为什么你要不理解仪表、不清楚状况地运营产品？(00:44:06): 我带的几乎每个团队——不管是 Instagram、Uber、Airtable、ChatGPT——我做的第一件事之一，总是——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I like about this growth team advice is that a lot of people think of a time to hire a growth team to we need to drive growth. What you're saying is there's a lot of second order benefits, which is they help you figure out what the hell's going on and inform a lot of other things that are happening, people just actually understanding how things are going.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个增长团队建议的地方在于，很多人以为雇增长团队是"我们需要驱动增长"的时候。你说的是有很多二阶好处：他们帮你搞清楚到底在发生什么、为很多其他正在发生的事提供信息，让人真正理解事情进展如何。

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: Totally. (00:46:38): I think that the reason why growth team is the advice I would go with rather than to build an analytics team is because if you build an analytics team or a data science team, it's possible that no one's going to listen to them. It's like, "Oh, I have these insights." It's like, "Well, no one really cares." (00:46:53): But if you hire a growth leader, they are now tied to outcomes of driving growth, so they're going to be the ones who are listening and asking more questions and really partnering with that data science team to make your entire product and business more rigorous. That just changes the DNA of your entire team.
turns.zh: 完全。(00:46:38): 我觉得我给"增长团队"这个建议、而不是"建分析团队"的原因在于，如果你建的是分析团队或数据科学团队，可能会没人听他们的。就像"哦，我有这些洞察"，然后"嗯，没人真在乎"。(00:46:53): 但如果你雇一位增长负责人，他们现在和驱动增长的结果绑定，所以他们会是那个在倾听、在问更多问题、并真正和数据科学团队搭档，让你的整个产品和业务更严谨的人。那只是改变了你整个团队的 DNA。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to talk about hiring, but is there anything else along these lines that you want to share of building new products, scaling products?
turns.zh: 我想聊招聘，但沿这条线你还有什么关于打造新产品、规模化产品的想分享吗？

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: I guess the last thing I would say is I want to make sure that sometimes in the pursuit of numbers, product folks lose sight of the importance of taste and craft. Maybe this is actually the dovetail into building teams, but you got to have the counterbalances. (00:47:39): It's really important to give two people on your team different charges. One is like go grow the product and the other one is wait, maintain that design, that beautiful aesthetic, the craft that your product is known for. That tension is extremely healthy. I've seen this at Facebook. I've seen this in Instagram. I helped create this at Instagram, this healthy tension. Airtable, same thing, but just having... ChatGPT, same exact thing. (00:48:11): You have to have that push and pull on both sides to really stretch the gamut.
turns.zh: 我想说的最后一点是，我想确保有时候在追逐数字的过程中，产品人忽视了品味和匠心的重要性。也许这其实能接到"建团队"上，但你必须要有反制力量。(00:47:39): 给团队里两个人不同的使命很重要。一个是去增长产品，另一个是等等，保持那个设计、那美好的美感、你产品赖以成名的匠心。那种张力极其健康。我在 Facebook 见过。我在 Instagram 见过。我在 Instagram 帮忙创造了这种健康张力。Airtable 一样，只是有……ChatGPT 完全一样。(00:48:11): 你必须两边都推、都拉，才能真正拉满整个区间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That begs the question, how do you actually do that? You could talk about it, you could be like, "Okay, we need to make sure the experience is awesome but also grow this number. Here's your goal." How do you operationalize that? Is it a performance review? Attribute thing? Is it culture or something else?
turns.zh: 这就引出问题：你到底怎么做到？你可以空谈，可以说"好，我们要确保体验很赞，同时也增长这个数字。这是你的目标。"你怎么把它落地？是绩效考核？归因？是文化还是别的？

turns.speaker: Peter Deng
turns.en: As a leader, you have to set up your team the right way. You have to really think about your team as a product and what are the various pieces you need to really stretch the gamut of what you're thinking about. (00:48:47): The teams that I've helped build are... The most successful ones are a team of Avengers that are just very different, have very different superpowers, but together you as the leader are the one who's helping adjudicate any differences or any disagreements but you know you're getting the best outcome when everyone's pulling and obsessing over a different thing. And that's important. (00:49:11): It's important to create your balance and really increase the space that you're looking at and create those healthy debates. (00:49:20): I think a lot of people overlook that. I think some people think of people on a team as warm bodies to do a job, but my philosophy has always been to think about, "Well, what does the company need to be successful and who's the best person who spikes at that one thing and how do I make sure that we get that person and how do we make sure we get the other person and the other person?" (00:49:43): It's almost like you're playing an RPG where everyone has different sliders and you have to create this super team where everyone actually spikes in different ways. (00:49:52): That is something that I've had a lot of success with in terms of when you create that environment and you create that vibe, you're going to get a lot of mileage out of that team.
turns.zh: 作为领导者，你必须用正确的方式搭建团队。你必须真的把团队当成一个产品来想——你需要哪些不同的部件，才能真正拉满你的思考区间。(00:48:47): 我帮忙建过的团队……最成功的，是一支复仇者联盟式的团队，成员非常不同、有非常不同的超能力，但作为领导者，你来裁定任何分歧或异议——但当每个人都在为一个不同的东西较劲、痴迷时，你知道你在得到最好的结果。那很重要。(00:49:11): 创造你的平衡、真正扩大你审视的空间、并创造那些健康的辩论，很重要。(00:49:20): 我觉得很多人忽视了这点。有些人把团队里的人当成干活儿的"人手"，但我的理念一直是想"公司要成功需要什么，谁是在那一件事上最拔尖的人，我怎么确保招到那个人，又怎么确保招到另一个、再另一个？"(00:49:43): 这几乎像你在玩 RPG，每个人有不同的滑块，你必须组建这支超强团队，让每个人真的在不同维度上拔尖。(00:49:52): 这是我在创造那种环境、那种氛围时，收获很大的一点——你会从那支团队得到很多回报。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is a really interesting answer. It's not one I've heard before. Essentially, it's not create the right incentives, it's hire people that naturally see the world in a certain way and that creates a balance and a healthy tension between say a PM and a designer and an engineer. And again, every place I've been at, as much as I've loved building the product, I've taken so much pride in building the team, and it's just been so much of a pleasure. And I think this is one of the two secrets that I have here.
turns.zh: 完全，完全。正是如此。话说回来，我 guess 我有两个关于招对团队想分享的点，很符合我的风格。我有个说法，其实有份文档我在各公司都带着走，叫 PXD API，大意是"怎么和我共事"。里面有句话，是我对所有我支持、我招的人最看重的，就是：六个月后，如果还是我在告诉你该做什么，那我就招错人了。这句话在三个层面上对我很有用。第一，它是我招聘或觅人时给自己的提醒，把标准抬得超高、绝不将就。因为如果我将就，六个月后很可能就不是"我能放手让这人跑"，而是我还在告诉他该做什么——那不是我要的。(01:03:07): 第二层效果是，我在人加入团队或我们决定录用时对他们说这句话，因为它传达了我的标准，也让他们知道怎样算成功、有个努力的方向。(01:03:26): 第三点是双方共同的，它给我们、让我和那人能在不同层面上运作——目标不是"你有没有完成这个 OKR、这个目标？"更高的目标变成：嘿，我们校准得够不够？我们是不是到了这样一种状态——六个月后，是由你告诉我该做什么？我们在朝那走吗？(01:03:55): 因为如果是这个框架，任何一方犯的错都成了学习机会：我们如何从这儿成长到六个月后想去的地方？作为管理者，我怎么做对的事帮这人成功，好让我六个月后不必介入？(01:04:20): 我觉得这三点，加上这句简单的话的二阶效应——"六个月后如果我在告诉你该做什么，我就招错人了"——给我压力、给那人压力，并创造了一种很有意思的环境、一个安全的空间去思考：我们朝那个目标走了吗？Again，我待过的每个地方，尽管我热爱做产品，我更以建团队为傲，那真是莫大的享受。我觉得这是我两个秘密之一。

turns.en: This is so good. I have a follow-up question, but just to point out why I think this is so genius is that there's kind a assumption here of this person, you can trust them. turns.zh: 这太好了。我有个跟进问题，但先指出为什么我觉得这很天才：这话里有个假设——你信任这个人。所以是"我信不信这人？我觉得他会主动吗？我觉得他会有正确的洞察力、也就是品味和直觉吗？"那是这个问题之下的那一层，很妙。而且这种自主权，几乎暗示了你想招的人的许多重要特质。我喜欢这个问题对你和他都如此简单[听不清 01:05:35]——

turns.en: I think this is for everyone. I think it's for everyone who is a manager. It's good for the person who is being brought onto the team, because they know what success looks like, and it gives them a path to keep on growing. turns.zh: 我觉得这是给所有人的。给每个管理者。因为如果你要在任何公司成为成功的管理者或领导者，如果你从一线经理做起、想成长，或只是想……如果你在公司早期，你有很多制度性知识。所以把学到的智慧传递出去、获得更多杠杆，对成功至关重要，我觉得每个管理者都该用这个思路对待下属。因为真的，对大家都好。对公司有更多杠杆和规模好。对加入团队的人好，因为他们知道成功长什么样、有路径持续成长。对你作为领导者、管理者也好，能放大整个团队的专业能力。

(01:08:50): Because I think it just creates this environment where everyone is open to what's the one thing I can get better at? And that whole get 1% better every day can become true. But I think the growth mindset thing is so important to me, that we build a org where people are self-reflective, and want to get better, and take that feedback, and give that feedback. At that point, it's hard to get feedback, it's hard to onboard to a new skill. It's hard to develop in any sort of meaningful way. And so I found that to be the really critical piece.
